utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the conflict, what was the ethnic makeup of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Baranja was made up of three ethnic communities in about an equal share. Croats, Serbs, and Hungarians each had one-third. There were other ethnicities represented to the extent of 1 or 2 per cent, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And prior to 1991, how were the relations between the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Considering that it was a multi-ethnic community, there was mutual tolerance and respect. There were mixed marriages. And since it is an agricultural region, farmers refrained from working during holidays, the holidays of another ethnic community. Generally speaking, there was a lot of mutual tolerance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 65 ter 5653. This is tab 57. That is not the exhibit I'm looking for. Let me see if I can ... It should be a map. And it's 5653. Ah, that's it. And if we could just enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm, is this a map of the Baranja region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you circle for us, using the pen that will be provided to you, Backi Breg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Backi Breg is here in this darker area. I cannot see it on this map. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was there a bridge nearby that entered into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was practically the only point of entry or exit into Baranja. It's at Batina. It's usually called Bezdan, although Bezdan is 3 to 4 kilometres away. It's marked here as a border crossing. Should I mark it nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why don't you put a B for bridge next to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you alluded to this just a moment ago. During the conflict, once the conflict broke out in Baranja, were there any other ways to enter or exit Baranja other than across this bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset of the conflicts - and I must add that they didn't break out in all of Baranja on the same day; however, it was within a short period that it happened - the Hungarian border initially was open. There is the border crossing of Udvar [phoen] which is also in the north of Baranja. It is marked here as a border crossing. There was also a ferry crossing west of the village of Jagodnjak, and you could go to Belisce there. In the first days of the conflict, it was possible to exit Baranja in the direction of Osijek. The bridge connecting Bilje - we can see Podravje [phoen] here on one bank and Osijek on the other bank - was mined. East of that bridge there was another bridge, a railroad bridge, which was operational. West of that bridge, there was a pedestrian bridge. But it couldn't carry heavy vehicles. It could be used by light vehicles and pedestrians though. In the first five to seven days after the conflicts broke out in Baranja, those were alternative points of entry or exit from Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that initially people could leave travelling I believe it's northwards from Beli Manastir into Hungary. When was that crossing closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crossing was closed when the Croatian police left Baranja, that is, Beli Manastir, because the police secured that crossing. I can't give you the exact date, but I suppose it was in mid-July or mid-August. After the Croatian police left, and they withdrew in the direction of Belisce, the border crossing with Hungary was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who blocked that exit point? What forces were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the Hungarian border police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And on the Croatian side, was there anyone blocking an exit from that check-point, or that entry point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the -- the TO of Knezevo took over that crossing, it was their duty to do that. But, of course, there's no logic in one country closing the border crossing and the other keeping it open because nobody can pass anyway. And, moreover, the crossing was mined. There were anti-tank mines laid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see on this map there's an X in the eastern part of Baranja. Can you tell us what's at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That entire area marked with a lighter shade is a natural park. And there was also the residence of Tito's palace, or Tikves palace. It was the former residence of President Tito and before him it was used by the king. It's a traditional facility for VIPs who came there to hunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And later on I'll be asking you questions about Grabovac. Could you circle that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more place to circle for us. You've already mentioned Bilje. Could you circle that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, after the 1990 elections, what was the most popular political party in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most popular party was the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of the members of the SDP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a multi-ethnic party. It -- even in its name there was no ethnic designation, and the people considered it as the most acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At some point, did another political party rise to prominence among the Serb population of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With time the SDS was able to attract more and more citizens of Baranja of Serbian ethnicity. On the other hand, the HDZ was able to do the same with ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us generally when did the SDS become -- rise in its popularity in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my assessment, the popularity of the SDS rose after the conflicts broke out in connection with the events at Plitvice and Borovo Selo. That is, starting from April or May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict in Baranja, so prior to July 1991, who was the leader of the SDS in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS leader was Ms. Vida Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And once the conflict began, did she remain in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe at the very beginning of the conflict but for a very short time because there were changes in the leading echelons of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who replaced her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic became the leader of the Baranja SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how did his views, how did Mr. Zivanovic's views compare to those of Ms. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could say that his views were more radical than those of Ms. Mandic. Although the objective was more or less the same, but they differed in their methods. His methods were more radical. He was in favour of proceeding faster, be more hands-on, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Within the SDS party structure in the 1991/1992 time-period, who was Mr. Zivanovic's superior within the SDS structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And focusing now in -- on the conflict period, what powers or influence did the SDS leadership exercise over municipal and village government in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structures of power were -- were pyramidal in form. The -- there was the municipality which had local communes. Practically each village was a local commune, and the local communes were subordinated to the municipal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to focus on the SDS leadership's, their powers, their influence over these local structures. What influence did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the influence was great and manifested itself in all aspects. From appointing the members of the Crisis Staffs to appointing the commanders of local TO Staffs within local communes. Those were the two most important factors when talking about Crisis Staff. Then there was the appointment and the removal of the management of companies. In other words, there was influence at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned the Crisis Staffs. What role did they play during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs are -- are a structure that was taken over from Yugoslavia. Its task or role was to react at times of crisis, any crisis, natural disasters included, but also war. Although in the plans that had been made, nobody expected this kind of war, but an aggression from with out. So the objective was to fight the enemy coming from another country. That's why the preparations were inadequate. And it became necessary to separate or the Crisis Staffs in -- rather, divide them into two aspects: The military component; and the civilian component that -- that would control other take -- be in charge of things that were not connected with mobilisation and military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that the SDS was involved in the appointment of TO commanders. Can you tell us, what criteria did the SDS use to select TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not asking the witness to speculate. It's if he knows what criteria was being used to select these TO commanders. I'm not going into in the details of the witness's background, but he does have some background in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So let's see whether he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, that law had been taken over from former Yugoslavia. The commanders of those Crisis Staffs were also the presidents of local communes. As I've mentioned, this proved inadequate. It became necessary to appoint a leadership for the military sector and another for the civilian sector. In the military sector, at the very beginning, people were appointed according to the ranks they had in the reserve force of the JNA. The higher rank somebody held the more likely it was that he would become the commander of the defence of his village. Then there were frequent -- there was frequent rotation resulting in people with poorer military skills as compared to some who would have been able to do the job better. But the one thing they had in common was that they were all SDS members.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware of -- and I want to talk now just briefly about the pre-conflict period. Were you aware of any politicians from Serbia coming to the Baranja region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Politicians became -- began coming to Baranja only after the conflict at Plitvice and Borovo Selo. I remember two politicians who came there, and that's Mr. Seselj and Mr. Paroski. They didn't come on the same day though. They came at different times. And the place they visited was Jagodnjak in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did they do when they came to Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They mostly organised rallies on a patriotic basis, ethnic awakening, and rising ethnic -- raising ethnic awareness among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the effect of these rallies on the relations between the ethnic groups in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position of Jagodnjak is specific because next to that village, there's the purely Croatian village of Ceminac and it was visited by Croatian politicians who had the same objectives. They also wanted to raise ethnic awareness. Jagodnjak had a Serbian majority. I think there were up to 80 per cent of Serbs among the population. And their tensions were rising between those two villages, and there was exchange of fire from infantry weapons, even -- there were even some mortar shells fired. And that was at -- at a time before the conflict broke out in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, prior to the conflict in Baranja, was the local Serb population supplied with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb population illegally got weapons after the events at Borovo. I don't know which quantity they got. The arming of the Serbs was stepped up only after the video in -- involving Martin Spegelj was shown on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where did these weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons had come from Serbia. As I've already said, it was transported illegally, although at the time the Croatian MUP had a check-point at the Batina bridge -- or a couple a months later, a kilometre and a half or 2 kilometres away from the bridge, on the road from Batina to Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who supplied these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and judging by the type of weapons that came in, and the -- those were old weapons, obsolete, if you will, and unused for a very long time. Those weapons had been in military warehouses. And according to what I learned later, it was distributed by the operatives of the KOG in Baranja villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when you refer to the KOG, do you mean the counter-intelligence group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Once the weapons arrived in Baranja, who was responsible for distributing them to members of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons were usually delivered to Jagodnjak village, and upon invitation, certain people who would be usually members of the SDS, and even higher-ranking people, would go there and bring back weapons into their own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when these persons collected these weapons and brought them back to their villages, what did they do in their villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They, in turn, would invite followers, supporters of the SDS, although by that time it stopped to matter that much. You would be invited if you were a Serb, whether you were a member or a supporter of the SDS or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were invited -- I'm reading your last answer. You were invited to come to these SDS members' location, and at that stage did they provide them with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it went. People would get an invitation to come to a remote place where the weapons were stored, and people would be given a time for collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, was there a Baranja TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a municipal TO Staff for Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was it headquartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was headquartered in Beli Manastir, like all the seats of political power and also the MUP and the Territorial Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict, who was the head of the Baranja TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who occupied the position of TO Staff commander in Baranja when all this started happening was Major --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you repeat the -- the name of the -- of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lazar Brnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was he at some point replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't exactly say when, but a month or a month and a half after the conflict broke out, he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His predecessor in that position, Borivoje Dobrokes. He used to be TO commander earlier, and then he retired from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who instituted this change in TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a political decision. The TO commander was appointed by local politicians, or, rather, the ruling party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was Dobrokes a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you know, could you tell us, was there a difference between Brnovic and Dobrokes, as far as their views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a difference. Brnovic was an organised man, very thorough, more liberal, whereas Dobrokes was short-tempered and much more radical, you can say, than Mr. Brnovic. A man of action. A man of the moment, impulsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you tell us, how was the Baranja TO structured? What was underneath it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure of the Baranja TO relied on two brigades. One was based in Beli Manastir; another in Darda. And there was a border detachment near Knezevo. Their area of responsibility was the border with Hungary. As far as the brigades are concerned, the Beli Manastir Brigade covered positions at the Drava river. That was the first separation line up from the north-west, a place called Torjanci. Down to the south up to the Topolik farm approximately, a cattle farm. From that Topolik farm via Bilje and partly Kopacki Rit was the area covered by the brigade in Darda. That was the so-called separation line, the first combat line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where did the village TOs fall within the structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on their geographic position, local staffs would be attached to a -- one of the brigades. Staffs of larger places provided personnel as needed. And larger places had to form battalions that would be part of the brigade; whereas, smaller places would form smaller units, beginning with the company, and larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware whether there was an SBWS TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, I apologise. The -- whether there was an SBWS TO. In other words, for the SAO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could be no two Territorial Defences. There was only one. I never heard that there was another parallel TO in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you're misunderstanding my question. Serb Autonomous District of the entire region of SBWS. So Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja. Were you aware that there was a TO at that level, at the SAO level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. That was only logical. It was an institution inherited from Yugoslavia by SAO Krajina. So it was present in its every form in that territory as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where was it headquartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in Slavonia. I'm not sure whether it was in Dalj or in Erdut. Considering that it was established before the liberation of Vukovar, it must have been in one of the places that was liberated earlier, such as Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the Baranja TO and this TO that was in Dalj or Erdut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can give you a good answer to that question because I did not personally monitor these contacts. And I didn't have any with the area of Slavonia. I can speak about anything that concerns Baranja. I'm not sure about Slavonia, how it worked. I can only make assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what level -- then let's return to Baranja. And if you tell us what level of armed conflict existed in Baranja in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is unclear what does it mean, what level? I don't know what does it mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is whether it was -- there was a significant amount of armed conflict there, or was it very little armed conflict. That is what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did. Let me see. In the first years of war, nor later, were there any large-scale direct conflicts. When I say "large scale," I mean those that would involve the movement of larger units. That did not happen in Baranja. You could say the conflict was local in nature, limited to one or two villages. The first major local conflict was the expulsion of Croat forces from Bilje village, and the second happened on 3rd February 1992, when the Croatian forces attacked the forward defence line near Torjanci village on the Drava river, and the conflict involved the stretch of 5, 6 kilometres of the forward line. The fighting would begin and end on the same day, and that's why I consider it a low-intensity conflict. There were no battles stretching over several days. There were no battles involving movements of larger units. Those were the few more important clashes that I remember. There were occasional incidents and breakouts and attempts to conquer the border crossings on the Hungarian border by members of the Croatian armed forces, but they were mostly unsuccessful, and these attempts usually ended in their surrender and capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think you alluded to this earlier. What happened to the Croatian members of the police at the beginning of the conflict in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian police abandoned Baranja. They pulled out from their base in Beli Manastir using a ferry towards Velisce [phoen] and Palvobo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did they leave Baranja voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before this happened, conflict had started in Karanac, Knezovi Vinogradi, and other places in Baranja. There were clashes in an increasing number of places including one in Beli Manastir between local Serbs and the Croatian MUP reserve. They had tried to infiltrate reservists by rail but word got out and this transport was intercepted. There was an exchange of fire involving losses on the Serbian side. But since all this was happening at the entrance to Beli Manastir, armoured transporters came out of the local JNA garrison and stopped this transport. Later on, maybe according to a directive from the Croatian government who had estimated that their personnel is in jeopardy, the police pulled out of Baranja. Except for Bilje village. They remained in Bilje village because it's 4 or 5 kilometres from Osijek, and they continued to operate safely for a while longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any ZNG units in Baranja when the conflict broke up -- broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the ZNG. But there were MUP units both from the active duty and the reserve force. However, it's possible there were ZNGs in Bilje village because they hailed from various parts of Croatia, Istria, Varazdin, et cetera. There were their men in Bilje. But their uniforms were different and it was difficult to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During the conflict in 1991, were any non-Serb villages taken over by Serb armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The territory of Baranja is rather idiosyncratic in terms of the ethnic distribution of the population. Several villages that were populated by Germans before the Second World War had been vacated and then resettled by population hailing from various parts of Yugoslavia. And during the resettlement, these villages became almost pure ethnically, with population from Medjumorje [phoen], Lika, Kordun, various other areas. And the villagers were -- the villages where these colonists were non-Serb were abandoned by that population. Only the Serbs and other non-Croats remained but they were few. After these villages were abandoned, they were mopped up. Territorial units and units from the MUP of Krajina went to search and mop up these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you just, for our benefit, name some of these villages that you mentioned in which the TO entered and mopped up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strategically speaking on the road those were Kozarac and Ceminac looking from Beli Manastir and Darda. The Serbs took over Beli Manastir and Darda and between those two larger places there are two smaller ones where the situation was not yet clear. The Croats had left, but not the entire villages had yet been taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did the non-Serb population in these villages offer any form of armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. First of all, the people who remained were too old and infirm. They stayed behind just to preserve their homes and estates. So there was no armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By the end of August 1991, what parts of Baranja remained outside of Serb control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic makeup of Bilje before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bilje, as a suburb of Osijek, which went through a sudden expansion just because of its vicinity to Osijek, a lot of people coming in from Osijek, the majority population was Croat, and there were many Hungarians. The Serbs had the smaller share in the population, perhaps 10 to 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was Bilje taken by Serb forces and if so when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb forces took Bilje, as I described earlier. It was one of the major operations. It was, in fact, the first large-scale military operation in the territory of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be precise. It could have been in August. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us which Serb forces participated in the takeover of Bilje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence and special police units from Beli Manastir and one special police unit from Knin, known as Kninjas. So the police was practically the main task force that went from house to house. The Territorial Defence kept Bilje surrounded, leaving a corridor for civilians and anyone who wanted to leave Bilje along the road that connects Bilje with Osijek. That was left open for the civilians to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who commanded the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Considering that the primary vehicle of the operation was the TO, the TO commander, Dobrokes, commanded the operation. He was man number one in the Territorial Defence. So he was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, this is our first break. We'll come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the court after we have gone into closed session. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you testified about the Croat colonist population in Baranja. Can you tell us, when did they abandon their villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've said that already. Before the Croatian police pulled out and when people learned that information, then the remaining non-Serb population of those villages started leaving Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I know dates are difficult for you, but can you tell us what month was that? Would that be July/August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them left in July or August. Late July, early August, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides this Croat colonist population were there, if I can use the term, indigenous Croats living in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there were indigenous Croats in Baranja. Some left, others stayed, but that changed daily. Some of them were making up their minds whether they should leave or not, and they -- it changed according to the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I believe the interpreters missed your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that, at the end, I said who joined the TO stayed. I'm talking about the non-Serb population. Those who would not join the TO were leaving or had the intention to leave Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we'll come to those issues in a moment. Could you tell us, this indigenous Croat population, what were the villages -- the main villages that they lived in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could be found in almost all villages. There weren't any ethnically pure villages. They were all mixed. In some villages, the Croats were the majority, and others the Hungarians and others, again, Serbs. But they were all mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And those villages where the Croats and the Hungarians and the other non-Serbs made up the majority, were those villages taken over by the Baranja TO in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The TO established staffs in each village or each local commune in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when those villages were taken over, was there any resistance by the non-Serb population during those takeovers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to briefly return to the attack on Bilje. Can you tell us -- you mentioned that the organiser would have been the Baranja TO commander, Dobrokes. Can you tell us, how was the attack organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plan to attack was agreed at the meeting between the TO commander, that is, Mr. Dobrokes and the commanders of the local TO Staffs. It took place at Jagodnjak. And the other participants were Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic and Mr. Djordje Latas as high-ranking SDS officials who were not military persons. At that meeting, it was agreed which local staffs should provide what number of men. Mr. Latas and Mr. Zivanovic were charged to provide materiel of non-military nature, such as transportation, logistics, and on all main directions ambulances were provided and medical staff, and the military component would provide -- was supposed to provide armaments, weapons and anything that has to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And prior to the attack on Bilje, had the Croat forces in Bilje mounted any significant attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from sporadic individual incidents, you can't -- you couldn't speak of an organised attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the significance of Bilje to the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- Bilje had a strategic significance. It was the only village in all of Baranja that was not under Serb control. And, secondly, in order to move the first line of defence in Baranja toward Osijek, you had to take Bilje. In front of Bilje, there's an old branch of the Drava river, and -- so that it was a very good defence line against a possible attack from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you may have alluded to this: How long did the combat operations in Bilje last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the attack on Bilje began at 5.30 a.m., and by 1.00 p.m. I think it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned before the break that a corridor was created from Bilje. Could you tell us, what happened to the non-Serb civilian population in Bilje during -- during or after the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the attack, in my opinion, most non-Serbs left Bilje. They were -- there were columns of vehicles, people were carrying their most precious belongings. Some non-Serbs stayed at Bilje. Only Bilje had a TO Staff which did not function there for the reasons that were mentioned already. It was physically impossible. Later on, it started operating in accordance with its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned also before the break a special police unit from Beli Manastir. Who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A special purpose unit established by the Beli Manastir SUP was commanded by Milan Jaric, an experienced police officer from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did any members of this unit receive training in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some members of that unit had previously been reserve police officers and then there were also some new arrivals, and all of them together underwent special training led by Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, were any problems caused by this special purpose unit during the takeovers of towns and villages in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit did cause problems. But Baranja was already practically under Serb control then. There was much property of non-Serbs who had left Baranja, such as business premises that certainly were interesting to some members of that unit. And that's why there was internal strife between them as well as conflicts with the non-Serbs who had stayed behind and owned some of the facilities that were interesting to them and some other property.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Besides property crimes, was this special unit committing other crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is said that some members committed murders while mopping up Kozarac and Ceminac. They mistreated and brought in mostly non-Serb inhabitants of Baranja to the SUP facility at Beli Manastir. There were such and similar occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, did any JNA units come to Baranja in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA had a permanently stationed unit from before the war. I believe I have mentioned it already. It was a unit that guarded the frontier, the border with Hungary, and it was stationed at Beli Manastir. It was the border garrison. As the events in Croatia unfolded, the 36th Subotica Brigade gradually moved into Baranja. It started by taking the bridge. I believe that I've also mentioned that the Croatian police forces took the Batina bridge in order to control traffic over the bridge. As the 36th Subotica Brigade advanced toward the bridge or -- which later became a bridge head, the check-points of the Croatian police retreated. That would -- began in 1991. And some units of the 36th Subotica Brigade were already -- were already present in Baranja then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give us roughly when -- when the 36th Brigade showed up in the Baranja region? Maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I mentioned it, the -- it was after the conflict at Plitvice and Borovo Selo. We can place it in the month of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did the JNA play in the takeover of villages and towns in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA did not take part in the takeover. It would sometimes be a buffer zone between the Croatian forces in Baranja and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When the local TO units entered a village or town in Baranja, what happened to the movable property of the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, there were different situations whether the Crisis Staff was immediately established or not. I mentioned the village Kozarac and Ceminac where there were no Crisis Staffs. There, looting began. Property was looted that could be taken away immediately, such as TV sets and smaller items. In villages, however, where there was a Crisis Staff, there were efforts to register such property, make a list of it, and seal those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where was the property that was taken -- where was it taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever was able to carry things took it home.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there more organised looting going on during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More organised looting began when it became necessary to provide transportation. It was for property that couldn't be carried by one man, so he needed a truck or a tractor to move it. And this is an agricultural region, so there was agricultural machinery. In other words, property that you can't even conceal, really. And there was a lot of living livestock left behind, from smaller animals all the way to cattle. Some people hid their property, but some of it was looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that some of this property was transported. Was any of it transported to outside the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was property that was taken to Serbia. And that was the only possible solution. Because on the other bank of the Danube in Serbia, the region is also agricultural. And it was very easy to resell agricultural machinery and such stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what part, if any, did the TO commanders play in this type of looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role and the objective of the commanders should have been to prevent that. But, at that time, objectively speaking, it was very difficult to do that. There were many people carrying weapons, in different moods, and it was extremely difficult. At any rate, they were unable to -- do that the way they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that they were unable. Did they participate in the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were situations when they gave in to temptation or whatever you may choose to call it. But there were situations when staff commanders made it possible and possibly even participated in what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now besides looting, when the TO entered into villages and towns, were they committing other crimes against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was pressure exerted on all non-Serbs, especially those whose family members had left Baranja previously, especially in the direction of Croatia. They were considered traitors and mistreated because their children or other relatives were members of the enemy army. That kind of pressure was continuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the effect of this pressure on the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were maltreated couldn't stand it long. And it went as far as people could bear. The -- those concerned eventually left Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on e-court 65 ter 267. This is tab 5. And I'm interested in the decision that's number 44. Which, I believe, is -- yes, on the right side of the -- the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a decision that's signed by Borivoje Zivanovic, dated 1 September 1991. And it states that: "Passes for leaving the municipality with a large quantity of goods or expensive goods may only be issued by the commander of the Baranja TO or a person he authorises." First of all, did the TO commanders exercise authority over the removal of property from the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we see, the commander of the municipal staff was able to transfer this authority and commanders of local staffs under this order, and they should have control over the -- over who of the local population leaves that place. I'm not sure, however, it was technically possible at the time. But certainly the local staff had to be informed of population movements in their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this deals with property movements. And you've testified that some TO commanders were complacent or even participated in some of the organised looting. What was the effect of giving this authority to TO commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I fully understand the question. But as for the looting of property, that refers to people who left Baranja without a permit, although there weren't any permits at that time. And whoever wanted to leave the region subsequently needed a list of property they wanted to take with them, and that was then controlled at the point of exit. Clearly those persons were unable to take away all their property and that again meant that the staffs had to be active because they also sealed abandoned houses. Now, of course, what they did specifically is something only those who were involved can know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What's -- was paperwork necessary to remove property from Baranja? To Serbia, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what we see, we know that this was required and checks were made, both at the staff and at the exit via the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it was the TO Staffs that were responsible for issuing that paperwork?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on e-court 65 ter 291.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I would object in the sense that, first of all, the witness should be asked about something. And then show him the document. Otherwise, it is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I believe this -- this document stems out of the evidence he's already provided with regard to takeover events in Baranja, and I simply want to compare some of the things that are stated in this document to what he knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a declaration on unconditional capitulation of Croatia in the area of Baranja. And it's a -- doesn't have a date on it, but there's a facsimile page with a date of 11 September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. May we see whose declaration is it? Who -- who issued this declaration. And who signed this declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's why I'm turning to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look under item 10 we see a number -- the persons who are listed as the signatories of this declaration. Are you familiar with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letters are too small. Could we make it larger? Just the passage you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just enlarge item number 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We have a technical problem for the moment, Mr. Olmsted. The technician is on his way. For the moment, we can't zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can make it out. Just a minute. Borivoje Zivanovic is mentioned in relation to Beli Manastir. And the commander of the TO Staff, Major Borivoje Dobrokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think that also -- that Vida Mandic is also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. In the second line of the second paragraph, under 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who were these individuals in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, it says president of the co-ordination board of Yugoslav-oriented parties, Dr. Vida Mandic who was president of the SDS; president of the Executive Board of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem for the municipality of Beli Manastir, Borivoje Zivanovic, also member of the SDS; and TO staff commander, Borivoje Dobrokes, also member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your recollection that those were the positions that they held in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I knew the exact position of Mrs. Vida Mandic after the rotation occurred in the leadership of the Baranja SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The others, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page -- we can't even turn to page 1 now. If we could just wait two minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention under -- of point 1 where it says that the whole area of Baranja is under the control -- or is controlled by the Territorial Defence and Beli Manastir municipality and SUP forces. Sir, is that consistent with your information about the -- the state of affairs as of September 1991, that Baranja was under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps can you help us out on this. It then mentions that there was a military administration in Beli Manastir for three days. Do you know, what are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not completely sure because it was a relatively short period, too short to leave much of an impression. Military administration. I'm not sure what these three days were. Was it a transition to normal operation of the authorities after the liberation itself? I can't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there ever a JNA military administration in Beli Manastir or in the Baranja region controlling civilian affairs or executive affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what a military administration would be, if the army had been governing all affairs. I'm not sure now. The JNA was present both with lower-ranking and higher-ranking commands, depending on the period. But I'm not sure about those two or three days. Perhaps it was a short period without any civilian authority. But I cannot claim anything with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you're not aware of a period when the JNA was governing Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look under point 4, it states that are there no paramilitaries in Baranja. You mentioned a number of units that were operating in Baranja. Were you aware of any paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not. And I believe there were no paramilitary units in Baranja. There had been attempts by adventurously bent individuals from Serbia to join individual staffs, but that was not tolerated and they were not admitted because they were not from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, was there a radio/television transmitter in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one, and it still exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to this transmitter after the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've stated before, some places were taken over by the Serbs, whereas others remained in the hands of the Croatian police. The TV transmitter remained part of the Croatian television. Although most of the places were in Serb hands, the TV transmitter still transmitted programmes broadcast by Television Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened to that transmitter in 1991? Did it remain in Croatian hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The TV transmitter was captured sometime in September. It was guarded by five armed men. And there was also one technician whose job was to take care of the quality and maintenance. When the men surrendered, the TV transmitter was switched off from the Croatian television and started broadcasting Belgrade, Novi Sad, and Subotica TV programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which Serb forces took part in taking over the transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the Territorial Defence from three different staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to play you a portion of a -- of a videotape. This is 65 ter 4967.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the sake of the translators, or interpreters, the transcript begins on page 5 of both the English and the B/C/S. And we're going to play beginning at 10 minutes and 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. My transcript doesn't run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your transcript ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think mine doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, should we just wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we could continue, couldn't we? Madam Registrar, as far as the Registry is concerned? Would it be okay with you, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately not because I cannot follow the same time video and the transcript on the same screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, yes. That's not possible. Okay. We'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think we can try to proceed, Mr. Olmsted. Is it all right with you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm just making sure that mine's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right now, it's not. But actually I'm perfectly fine working without it at this stage just so we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We were told to close it and re-open it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that works.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's good advice. And that advice works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes. And just so we're back on the record, this is 65 ter 4967, tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'd like to play, sir, a video for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] May I -- let's just clarify the issue of the Croatian TV rating. I assume it could be watched since it is connected to the transmitter at Bilje. In this connection, the Croatian television has sent a letter to television Novi Sad demanding that they return the transmitter. We answered that this transmitter is theirs if they wanted and as far as we are concerned they can use it. "Goran Hadzic: It is absurd that they're asking you to return it. Baranja has been liberated. Ustashas have been expelled. Everything that remained on Baranja territory of the people who remained there, it means the Serbs, Hungarians, and Slavonians who did not do anything wrong. It's absurd. Our units took over the transmitter. They liberated it and it's normal for us to decide which program to broadcast. I mean, this is an absurd issue. Even Goebbels is an amateur comparing to what the Croatian TV does, and that we permit them to be watched through this transmitter, I mean ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us who was the man wearing the yellowish suit that answered the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Mr. Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And he mentions our units took over the transmitter. What is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's talking about the capture of the transmitter carried out by three units or, rather, units from three staffs of the Territorial Defence of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, why was the Baranja transmitter significant to the SAO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view, it was significant for two reasons. One is that Croatia was spreading propaganda using that transmitter, and it was necessary to prevent the spreading of Croatian propaganda in territories under Serb control. And, secondly, with the help of these studios whose programmes were taken over, it was necessary for news and programmes in Baranja to be broadcast from Serb-held territory. Another important thing is the strategic position of the TV transmitter. After it was taken over, the JNA installed a complex radar system there because it's the highest elevation in the radius of about 50 kilometres. So it had a dual use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us what area was covered by the transmitter? What -- what geographical area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That whole geographic area. In Baranja, it is located at an elevation called Baranja mountain at the highest point, at some 400 metres of altitude. So the top of the transmitter is 450 metres tall, if you include its own height. Which means that it has a very large range.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did it cover Eastern Slavonia as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eastern Slavonia, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after the takeover of the transmitter, where did the broadcasts through the transmitter come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the early days, the entire programme was taken over from TV Serbia. And then gradually news programmes were introduced from Baranja that the Beli Manastir studio had managed to prepare in the course of the day to cover the developments in Baranja itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what happened to Croatian broadcasts through the transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian broadcasts were no longer transmitted from the day the transmitter was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this video be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2155. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were eventually broadcasts made from Baranja from Beli Manastir. Where was that studio located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the centre of Beli Manastir, there is a recent building called P+8. In that building, there is a TV studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did any political parties exercise influence over what was broadcast through the transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS was the leading political party in Baranja. And there was no real opposition, but if you wanted to call a party that it would be the Serbian Radical Party. The programme was influenced by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 525 on the screen. This is tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I think that the translation was not correct because witness said, "I consider that the programme was influenced by the SDS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you check that with the witness, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to confirm your last answer, the transcript reads: "The programme was influenced by the SDS." And Defence counsel was asking whether you, in fact, said, you considered it to be influenced by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It was not my question, but that's something that witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Can you repeat your last answer regarding the SDS and its influence over the programming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I thought the SDS had influence because who appointed the director of the television and the editors and all the way down to the camera staff and reporters? It was exclusively in a part of the SDS's authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have on the screen 65 ter 525 which is an article in the "Vreme" newspaper from 4 November 1991. The first paragraph deals with the takeover of the Baranja transmitter, which you've already told us about. If you could look at the third paragraph, the article notes that: "Viewers are greeted by authorised civilian officials identifying themselves as announcers." Sir, do you recall seeing civilian officials over the station and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. Those -- in those early days, it was difficult to see a civilian anywhere. Everybody was wearing some kind of a uniform, either a camouflage uniform or an old JNA uniform that was issued by the TO. Daily life was not very orderly. Whoever wore weapons or not was wearing some kind of uniform. I don't really remember seeing a civilian in those first days. Maybe I didn't watch long enough, but certainly I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall any political leaders from the Baranja region providing information over this local station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning, the president of the Executive Council of the Beli Manastir municipality, Mr. Zivanovic, briefly presented the events of the day or possibly some plans. There would be reports on attempted breakthroughs or provocations on the front line and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you consider the information being provided through the local station to be objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe not all of it. It was a problem to estimate what was a serious attempted breakthrough and who provoked who because all sorts of things went on, on the front line. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You've already mentioned some of the crimes being committed against the non-Serb population in 1991. Was any information about those crimes broadcast over the local station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I must say that I didn't spend much time watching TV due to the circumstances under which I lived and worked. But I don't remember information about crimes or sanctions against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5, the article reports Hadzic as stating that 95 per cent of the assembly delegates were SDS members. I believe you already touched on this issue. Was there a significant opposition in the assembly during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can now only interpret what I see, although I did mention that this was another party in Baranja, that's the Radical Party, which was in opposition to some extent, although their common goal was the liberation of the Serbian people in all territories. Now the question is of course what you can consider an opposition. Possibly the radicals didn't agree with all aspects of personnel policy. But I don't think there was a real opposition with a different idealogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just number-wise, was there a large number of opposition members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, it is important to know which period we're talking about. Because the numbers varied. The SDS was certainly the strongest, most numerous party in the region. Now, the radicals sometimes rose over 5 per cent. Maybe they reached as high as 15 per cent. But then it depends on the time-period in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, that's a noteworthy clarification. I'm talking about the period of this article, so November 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that this is realistic. It -- I don't know the statistical data, and this is all about statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this article be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object. First of all, we do not know the author of this article. On the other side, witness could not provide any significant answer about this specific issues from this article. And I would say that this -- the author, this article, just demonstrates the bias of the author towards Mr. Hadzic. And I -- there is not any citation from his -- from his statements or something like that, so I would oppose to -- to admitting of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The author that -- they provide the initials of the author of this article. We obviously have a -- an original copy of the article taken from the "Vreme" periodical with the date on it. And we submit it relates to the evidence presented by this witness thus far with regard to the transmitter in Baranja, and the local broadcasts that were made over that transmitter during the period in question. As far as the bias in the article, I think we have to leave that up to, you know, the Trial Chamber taking that into consideration when it decides what weight to give this, but it does corroborate the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just add that the takeover of the transmitter was asked and answered by the witness with the -- and this document does not help -- help us to -- to understand anything else, but it contains many many other -- many other points that, in my view, are not -- are not reason for -- for -- for admitting of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may respond to that, Your Honours. It -- it goes beyond the transmitter. It goes to the witness's evidence regarding local programming, the existence of this local broadcasts that were coming out of the Beli Manastir area after the transmitter was taken over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Mr. Witness, we'll take our second break. We'll come back at 1 -- at 12.45. And, as soon as we are in closed session - closed session, please - the court usher will escort you out of court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, after the outbreak of the conflict in Baranja, who was the head of the Beli Manastir SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leadership, that is, the chief and the secretary, Svetislav Vranic was the chief and Radoslav Zdjelarevic was the secretary. These are the first two men of the Beli Manastir SUP. Number one and number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, who was number one and who was number two as far as hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In hierarchical terms the secretary of the SUP is number one and the chief is number two, he is a pure operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not going to attempt to say the secretary's name. So let me just ask you, can you tell us when was he appointed to his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Beli Manastir SUP began to function once the Croatian police had left. The -- I can't give you the exact date, but as soon as the Croatian police left the building, the Beli Manastir SUP - that is to say, the Serbian SUP of Beli Manastir - was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how many police stations reported to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, there was the milicija station at Darda and the SUP at Beli Manastir. As events developed in Baranja, there was a need to cover the entire territory. There was another milicija station at Batina, and they controlled the border crossing, that is, the bridge at Batina. Then there was another at Knezevi Vinogradi and another at Bilje. Beli Manastir, Dardik, Knezovi, Vinogradi, Bilje, and Jagodnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And by August 1991 what was the ethnic makeup of the police force in Baranja? You already mentioned that the Croat police had left. What was the ethnicity as of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police was made up of the people who had stayed in Baranja. Most of the staff of the Beli Manastir SUP were Serbs. A smaller number of Croats had stayed. They were police officers before. And a couple of Hungarians too. The percentage of non-Serbs at the Beli Manastir SUP certainly did not exceed 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to now ask a series of questions regarding the conditions in Baranja faced by the non-Serb civilian population from July 1991 through 1993. But to help us out, first, could you break this time-frame into different periods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In rough terms, this can be divided into a number of periods. The period from the start of the conflicts, that is, June, July, August, when there was a sudden change of the ethnic structure of the population. And there was uncontrolled arming. Whoever wanted could take up arms, and it was very difficult to exercise any sort of authority at the time. When civilian authorities and the TO Staff and the SUP starting functioning in Beli Manastir and other institutions too, life was slowly going back to normal. Again, that depended on the events on the ground, whether or not there were mass expulsions of Serbs from Western Slavonia because that provoked similar reactions on the other side and vice versa. Speaking about refugees, let me mention that in late 1991 and in 1992, up until March or so, there was a massive organised influx of refugees who had been expelled from Western Slavonia and had reached Serbia by way of Bosnia. In Baranja, there were vacant houses belonging to Croats or other non-Serbs who had left Baranja, so they were trying to put these houses -- make these houses available to these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'll go into further detail regarding these periods in a moment. But I just want to set a framework here. As I understand it, there was an initial first period from June to sometime in August, and then you mentioned at that there was a second period, once the SUP in Beli Manastir and TO Staff began to fully function. Can you tell us roughly when that second period began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can say that it was as of mid-September or end September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, if I understand it, there was a third period in which there were a number of Serb refugees coming into Baranja, and that was beginning late 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Round about December 1991, the first refugees appeared. That is, in an organised fashion. Refugees had been coming to Baranja from July, but in Western Slavonia, Serbs were expelled and they were staying in Serbia provisionally but they were looking for a more permanent solution, and Baranja seemed a solution with prospect for the coming period because there were many empty houses and most of these people were able to settle in the same village as their former co-villagers so that social relations could be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first want to address this initial period, this first period, beginning June and going through August. Can you tell us -- obviously you've already testified that this was the period when there was the takeovers of the villages and other events. What were the conditions like for the non-Serb population during this first period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not good. Especially for those who had a family member or a friend who was -- who -- an immediate participant in the Croatian forces or who had a child who had left Baranja because whoever had left Baranja at that time was considered to have joined the Croatian army, which was not necessarily the case. But that was the prevailing view. And so whoever stayed and had someone who had left Baranja were under constant pressure because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you mention pressure. Were they subjected to crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the most serious form of pressure. There had been incidents. There were murders, expulsions. After each murder, there would be more people moving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this initial period, did the police take any measures to prevent these crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think anybody took any measures. It was a time of anarchy and general euphoria. Everybody was afraid of everyone else. Everybody was armed and prepared for anything. It was difficult to keep control over such large numbers of people under arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When the situation calmed down later on in 1991, did the police investigate any of these crimes committed during this early period, this June through August period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What does it mean to investigate a crime? The police would come to the crime scene when bodies were found, for instance, and they would collect some information. They would be able to identify the victim, the location, et cetera, but there was no follow-up. Criminal reports would be filed against an unidentified perpetrator and that would be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During this first period, were non-Serbs being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it was a period when anarchy reigned. Anybody with a weapon would be able to make an arrest, and nobody was safe from arrests in that situation where practically every armed person could arrest someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you say "anybody." Was it anybody or were they the non-Serbs who were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, it would be non-Serbs because at that time they were considered an enemy and a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us when did these arrests begin? What month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the remand prison of the Croatian SUP, once the police left the building that included the prison premises, those prisons were used to keep, to hold the people who were suddenly being arrested in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the record, you refer to the Croatian SUP. Would that be also the Beli Manastir SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said when the Croatian police left the SUP in Beli Manastir the building remained empty, the SUP of Beli Manastir had not yet been formally established, and everybody wearing a uniform was trying to arrest somebody and bring them to that remand prison at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified that "...everybody wearing a uniform." Would that include members of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant primarily members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us, to the extent you know, why were non-Serbs being arrested during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For all sorts of reasons, including trivial ones. First of all, anybody who was a member of the HDZ was an enemy. Anybody whose family member was of the HDZ was an enemy.
